newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico passes controversial political reform bill.
newsitem.headline: Mexico passes controversial political reform bill.

text.p: Mexico's ruling party legislators passed a controversial electoral reform bill early on Friday after watering down key provisions aimed at fairer elections and sparking the wrath of opposition parties.

Lawmakers of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) used their majority to pass the bill by a 282-142 margin. Every PRI legislator but one voted in favour of the bill and every opposition politician voted against it, officials said.

The bill was the product of nearly two years of painstaking negotiations between the parties and was backed heavily by Zedillo, who wants to trumpet cleaner elections as a step toward greater democracy in a country with notoriously dirty polls.

But PRI deputies, normally presidential political pawns, staged a surprising rebellion on Wednesday, making last-minute changes to the bill in a bid to ensure their party extends its 67-year grip on power.

The changes guaranteed the reform bill would pass without a seal of approval from the opposition, which have made unheard-of gains against the PRI in recent elections due to Mexico's economic crisis and a string of PRI corruption scandals.
Among other things, PRI deputies altered the electoral reform bill so that:
-- exceeding campaign spending limits would no longer be an electoral offence, only an "administrative error"
-- coalitions between opposition parties would be severely restricted
-- plans for a special body to audit party finances in campaigns would be scrapped.
Opposition lawmakers said the rebellion by ruling party legislators against Zedillo shows that hardliners in his party are determined not to surrender power.

"This is a blow to Ernesto Zedillo," said Alejandro Gonzalez Alcocer, a deputy for the right-wing PAN opposition party. "The hardline group of 'dinosaurs' in the PRI are trying to stop (reform) at all costs."
For the main left-wing opposition party, the PRD, deputy Graco Ramirez described the PRI's about-face as "a vote of fear, fear of democracy."
PRI deputies were in a defiant mood on Thursday as the Chamber of Deputies debated the bill's second and final reading.
"This is not a matter for the president of the republic," said PRI legislator Jorge Moreno. "This is what we want."

Such fighting talk is common in countries with more independent legislatures but almost unheard-of from the PRI, created after the 1910-17 Mexican Revolution to serve as the institutional arm of the all-powerful presidency.
Early on Friday, PRI deputies defended their actions in a statement, saying they refused to be "blackmailed" by opposition parties.

PRI legislators on Thursday admitted their party had been upset by heavy losses in town hall elections on Sunday and feared it might lose its majority in Congress when Mexico elects legislators in next July's mid-term elections.
There was no immediate reaction from Zedillo, who was scheduled to return to Mexico City late on Thursday after visiting Argentina when the deputies launched their rebellion.
